summary: Weekly POC sync focused on smoothing throughput variance using continuous batching and shaping concurrency; agreed next steps for load run and artifact sharing; some confusion around queue depth and buffer sizing resolved in principle but requires bench testing.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-20 16:00 UTC | Duration: 47 min | Attendees: Sofia, Marco, Anya (Redwood); Priya, James, Tasha, Evan (Meridian)

[00:00] Sofia Patel: Okay cool, um alright everyone thanks for joining, this is the weekly pilot sync for the Merid— Meridian throughput POC, quick agenda: results recap, tuning we did this week, and next-load plan. Marco, you wanna start with the numbers?

[00:20] Marco Rivera: Yeah sure, I'll run through it. So we ran the two 45-minute bursts on Tuesday and Thursday, mixed short prompts (~32 tokens) and long prompts (~512 tokens). Aggregate tokens per second peaked at about 2.7k on the Thursday run, average was ~1.9k. P50 latency for generate calls was around 130ms, p95 hovered 420 to 480ms depending on the burst. There was a visible tail when concurrency spiked.

[00:48] Priya Nair: Wait p95 480, that was with caching on or off? I thought we had prefix cache enabled for short prompts.

[00:58] Marco Rivera: Right — on Thursday we enabled prefix cache for keys with frequency > 5, but we had a small bug where one of the prefixes wasn't matching because of leading whitespace in the prompt, so effective cache hit-rate was 18% not the expected 32%, so tail was worse.

[01:18] James Elliot: That whitespace thing, we see that a lot in our preproc, so probably on our side too, we'll strip. Good catch.

[01:25] Marco Rivera: Also, queue_depth was set to 64 for the host pool and we were seeing queueing backlog when client concurrency hit 24 threads. The runtime's continuous-batching merged a lot of requests into 32-40 token batches for short prompts, but the mix with long prompted increased per-batch time.

[01:46] Tasha Green: Can you explain continuous-batching again? I thought batching only happens when requests come in very close together.

[01:53] Marco Rivera: Yeah, so continuous-batching in our runtime holds an open micro-window — usually 10-25ms — it aggregates incoming tokens across requests for the same model shard and issues a single kernel launch. That reduces per-token overhead, but it can add a few ms of waiting which shows up on tight latency SLOs for single-turn short queries.

[02:11] Priya Nair: So is there a knob to prioritize short queries to avoid them getting stuck behind a long one? We need consistent 150ms median for short prompts.

[02:20] Marco Rivera: Two levers: 1) route short-prompt traffic to smaller sequence-length-optimized slices (model variant quantized and shorter max-seq) — that lowers compute per request; 2) set concurrency targets + queue prioritization so short queries get priority and long queries go to a background queue or separate pool.

[02:40] Eva(n) [sic] Cho: Sorry Evan here — question on autoscaler behaviour, when you say 'separate pool' is that Redwood Dedicated or just a separate shard? How does burst capacity work?

[02:50] Sofia Patel: Good question. For the pilot we're on Redwood Hosted but Dedicated-style pooling is simulated by pinning shards to N GPUs. Burst capacity is an optional buffer we can enable — it'll spin up pre-warmed instances up to X for short windows but note there's cost and a cold start tail if we exceed burst.

[03:08] Anya Lowe: Also note the fallback policy we discussed: if p95 > 600ms, traffic routes to a lower-cost model variant automatically. That keeps apps responsive while maybe lowering quality slightly.

[03:20] Priya Nair: Hmm, we'd need to understand quality delta. Our evals are sensitive. Any way to auto-sample and re-eval outputs?

[03:30] Marco Rivera: Yes, Redwood Optimize will auto-sample a percentage of requests and run evals against your reference set, it can trigger alerts if quality drops beyond a threshold. We'll set that up for the next run.

[03:42] James Elliot: From infra side, we hit an interesting pattern: when concurrency increased beyond 18, GPU kernel saturation increased but we also saw more outliers — seemed like per-request queueing jitter. Could be related to our client retry patterns. Evan, are you adding jitter?

[03:55] Evan Cho: We don't add significant jitter right now, it's a fixed retry 500ms backoff, we're open to adjusting.

[04:02] Marco Rivera: For retries it's often best to use an exponential backoff with random jitter, otherwise you get synchronized bursts that cause spikes in batch windows.

[04:12] Sofia Patel: Quick pause — we should capture concrete next-run config: concurrency target (clients) of 16, queue_depth 64 vs 128 test, continuous-batching window 20ms, enable prefix cache after whitespace normalization, and sample 5% for offline eval. Everyone good?

[04:29] Priya Nair: Yes, 16 concurrency sounds fine. Question though: what's the expected per-token cost change if we enable smaller sequence-optimized variant for shorts?

[04:38] Marco Rivera: Roughly 20-30% lower per-token GPU cost for short sequences because kernel paths are faster and quantization yields better throughput. But you'll trade a small delta in generation quality depending on prompt.

[04:50] Tasha Green: On security — we have to sign off SOC2 and KMS. Did you already send the security pack?

[04:58] Sofia Patel: I attached the SOC2 summary and KMS integration notes in the pilot folder, but I'll re-send the full pack and the private deployment checklist. For on-prem or VPC we can talk privately with your security team.

[05:10] Priya Nair: Good. Also another ask: our product needs deterministic latency under 200ms 95% of the time for short prompts or we'll have to fallback to our own minimal local model. Does Redwood support hard SLOs?

[05:21] Marco Rivera: We offer latency SLOs in Dedicated plans — you can set soft limits in Hosted and Redwood will provide routing and fallback guidance. For hard SLOs we usually recommend Dedicated/reserved capacity with a small buffer and the burst pre-warm option.

[05:36] James Elliot: For the test we also want to try a scenario where short queries are pinned to a smaller shard at a 2:1 ratio to long queries, to see if segregation helps tail.

[05:47] Marco Rivera: Yeah that's one of the top recommendations. We'll simulate a pinned pool for short sequences and run A/B.

[06:01] Priya Nair: Anything on the memory side? We saw some OOM warnings on the Thursday run when many long sequences came in.

[06:10] Marco Rivera: Those were related to KV cache growth + three long sequences in-flight — we can cap per-session KV cache size and evict LRU at lower thresholds to avoid OOM. Also kernel memory thresholds can be tuned.

[06:22] Evan Cho: Can Redwood expose those memory metrics to our Prometheus endpoint?

[06:27] Anya Lowe: Yes, we can stream per-shard metrics and traces to your Prometheus with the agent; we'll share the manifest.

[06:35] Tasha Green: One more enterprise question — audit logs for data residency and KMS usage: are they tenant-scoped?

[06:41] Sofia Patel: Yes tenant-scoped audit logs, and key operations are recorded. We'll provide the example KMS rotation policy and audit format.

[06:48] Marco Rivera: Back to tuning — we've recommended three experimental knobs for next-run: 1) queue_depth 64 vs 128; 2) continuous-batching window 10ms vs 20ms; 3) shard segregation for shorts and longs. We'll log per-run p50/p95/p99 and tokens/s.

[07:10] Priya Nair: Sounds good. For the reported results — the Thursday run where we saw 2.7k tokens/s peak, what was the effective throughput for user requests per second (RPS)?

[07:19] Marco Rivera: Effective RPS was ~140 for the mixed mix, because long requests consumed more tokens. But short-only it's approx 220 RPS.

[07:28] James Elliot: We're concerned about cost at those RPS numbers. Is there an obvious leverage to reduce cost without hurting latencies?

[07:35] Marco Rivera: Short answer: yes, reduce model size/quantize for short-query pool, and use prefix caching aggressively once you clean prompt normalization; both reduce tokens/inference cost and improve throughput. Also batching increases throughput — continuous-batching reduces per-request overhead but must be tuned not to blow latency SLOs.

[07:50] Priya Nair: Ok let's run the 2-hour mixed workload on Monday/Wednesday (you said 22nd earlier) — what's the window again?

[07:59] Sofia Patel: Proposed 2026-03-22 02:00-04:00 UTC to align with your low-traffic window. We'll run both queue depth configs and push logs to the sandbox account.

[08:09] Evan Cho: We'll add exponential jitter to retries and we'll strip whitespace client-side before sending.

[08:15] Marco Rivera: Great. I'll also enable 5% sample evals and set alerts if p95 exceeds 450ms for short pool.

[08:22] Sofia Patel: Any blockers from Meridian?

[08:25] Priya Nair: Need to get the prompt sets to you and confirm the SSO scoping. Also need a ballpark cost estimate for two-week pilot extrapolated to steady-state.

[08:34] Sofia Patel: I'll send a pilot cost estimate today and the security pack.

[08:38] Tasha Green: Cool. Anything else?

[08:40] Sofia Patel: Quick recap of next steps: Marco runs A/B and pushes flags; Priya sends prompts and histograms; Evan tweaks retries and shares autoscaler; Sofia sends cost & security docs; follow-up deep-dive Thursday to discuss buffer sizing if early runs show tails.

[08:58] James Elliot: Thanks everyone.

[09:01] Sofia Patel: Thanks all, we'll sync after the run. Bye.

Notes: transcript has occasional mislabels (Evan spelled 'Eva(n)' earlier), minor ASR errors (e.g. 'de-dedicated' sometimes heard), timestamps approximate.
